newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE-Timeless Buddhist chants echo across Kandy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Timeless Buddhist chants echo across Kandy.

text.p: The timeless chant of Buddhist monks floats across the water. The throb of Kandyan drums reverberates around the lake.

A full moon shines gently down on the temple's golden roof as crickets chirrup in the cool night air. At sunrise, the religious devotions begin again as the sweet smell of incense pervades the Temple of The Tooth.

Dalada Maligawa is one of the holiest Buddhist shrines in the world. Here lies the sacred tooth of the Buddha, a revered symbol of sovereignty that is paraded around Kandy once a year on the back of an ornately decorated elephant. SACRED RELIC THAT FEW EVER SEE
Few ever see the sacred relic hidden deep in seven caskets of gold and silver. The entrance is framed by two giant elephant tusks.
At the weekly ritual washing of the relic, a monk pours water on a mirror in front of the tooth. It is too holy to touch. The tooth is revered as every word that Buddha spoke touched it.
It was brought to Sri Lanka in the fourth century, hidden in a princess' hair to keep it safe from marauders.
Visitors to the temple can go no further than the Hall of Beatific Vision, an antechamber where they may view from a distance.

A sign hanging over the altar in the moated temple tells them: "Abstinence from all evil, performance of all good, governance of one's mind. It is the teaching of the enlightened one." DAWN IS A MAGIC TIME
Dawn is a magic time to visit the temple in Kandy when just a handful of worshippers are kneeling in prayer.
Serenity pervades the temple as orange-robed monks pad off to their devotions.
At the temple next door, a monk pores over the tablets of holy scripture but pauses politely to greet the visitor from abroad.
Out comes a photo album showing the tour he took of European Buddhist centres.
One of the more incongruous images is a photo of him in France posing outside the EuroDisney theme park, his orange robes wrapped in an overcoat, his shaven head covered by a woolly hat.
The visitor is formally blessed for a safe journey home, his donation slipped into the alms box. Money must never touch the hand of the monk himself. A TOWN SO SWEET TO ITS PEOPLE
Sri Lanka's cultural capital is nestled in Hill Country foothills and fringed by a lovely tree-lined lake. Mist rises at dawn from the jungle behind.
Kandy is indeed sweet to its 100,000 people but the name in fact means "Hill" in Sinhalese.
It maintained independence from British, Dutch and Portuguese colonisers until finally succumbing to the British in 1815.
It was World War Two headquarters for Lord Mountbatten before Sri Lanka won independence from Britain in 1948.
Beside the inner temple stand two bare-chested Kandyan drummers, beating out insistent rhythms that echo round the antechamber's richly painted walls. KANDY DANCERS TWIRL LIKE WHIRLING DERVISHES
Their hypnotic beat echoes out every night when visitors to a more prosaic setting are treated to an hour-long display by the Kandy Lake Club Dance Ensemble.
This is a far cry from the genteel rhythms of a western ballroom.
Here richly attired dancers in glistening breastplates and jangling anklets juggle with fire and somersault in the air like whirling dervishes.
The hips of the women dancers sway, their hands gliding to simulate the graceful movements of the peacock.
The men in richly coloured masks enact a fiercely fought battle between a cobra and a bird.
"This dance is used to exorcise demons from the possessed and is still believed to be effective psychiatric treatment in Sri Lanka," the guide explains.

Then comes the interval, given a surreal touch in the Lake Club. Visitors may join club members in a game of roulette or watch horse racing from England carried live by satellite television to inveterate Sri Lankan gamblers.
You are then transported abruptly back to the more exotic realms of the past.
The fire-eaters roll blazing flames across their tongues and then stride across a bed of burning coals without a glimmer of pain on their faces.
It is all a question of mind over matter as they enact how the power of fire can drive out the 27 devils said to trouble mankind.
For, as the guide explained: "The absolute faith of the dancers protects them from the flames."
